lesson_title: Round Up or Round Down? The Question That Decides the Mark
hook_text: 9,47 litres of paint means buy 10. 5,47 days of water means you get 5. Same decimal, opposite answers.
clip_script: Here is the thing nobody tells you about measurement questions: the maths is the easy part. It's the last step that decides the mark. Paint the back room: you work it out and you need 9,47 litres. Do you buy 9? No — you go UP. You cannot buy 0,47 of a tin, and coming home half a tin short means a second trip and a wall that doesn't match. Now the water tank. It holds 2 463 litres, the family uses 450 a day, so 2 463 divided by 450 is 5,47 days. Do you go up to 6? No — you go DOWN. That sixth day runs dry halfway through. Same decimal, opposite decisions. So the rule is not about the number at all, it is about the situation. Materials round UP, because you must have enough. Days and whole items round DOWN, because you cannot have part of one. Ask which kind you are holding, every single time — that is the mark.
visual_style: Split screen: a paint tin filling past a 9,47 line and clicking to 10 with an up arrow, against a water tank draining across five full sunrises and stopping mid-way through a sixth with a down arrow.
mood: Practical, slightly conspiratorial — the tip nobody gave you.
pacing: Quick hook, two clean contrasting beats, firm rule at the close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson for fencing, tiling and tank calculations in rands.
